title: Mango Chia Pudding With Cardamom and Saffron: A Five-Minute Indian-Inspired Breakfast
excerpt: This no-cook recipe combines ripe mango with cardamom, saffron, and pistachios — classic Indian dessert flavors in a wholesome make-ahead breakfast format.
body:
• This Indian-inspired mango chia pudding combines ripe mango with cardamom, saffron, and pistachios for a no-cook breakfast or dessert that takes just five minutes to prepare.
  • The recipe uses Ataulfo mangoes blended with milk and aromatic spices, then mixed with chia seeds and refrigerated until thick and creamy — no stovetop or oven needed.
  • Chia seeds provide 10 grams of fiber per serving alongside protein and omega-3 fatty acids, making this a nutritionally dense alternative to traditional Indian sweets.
  • The dish can be meal-prepped for up to four days and customized with coconut milk, Greek yogurt, or different nut toppings.

Mango season in India means one thing: the fruit finds its way into everything. From lassis and milkshakes to kheer and shrikhand, the marriage of ripe mango with cardamom and saffron runs deep through Indian culinary tradition. Now, that same flavor profile is finding a new vehicle — chia pudding.

The recipe, shared by Delhi-born food writer Aneesha Gupta of Spice Cravings, transforms the familiar Indian dessert combination of mango, cardamom, and pistachios into a wholesome make-ahead breakfast. It requires no cooking, no special equipment beyond a blender, and just five minutes of active preparation.

How It Works

The process is straightforward. Half a cup of chopped ripe mango — preferably the buttery, less fibrous Ataulfo variety — is blended with milk, a quarter teaspoon of freshly ground cardamom powder, and a teaspoon of maple syrup. The resulting puree is poured into a jar, and two tablespoons of chia seeds are stirred in along with a pinch of saffron strands.

""As chia seeds absorb liquid, their soluble fiber forms a gel-like coating," she explains."

The critical step, according to Gupta, is the second stir. "As chia seeds absorb liquid, their soluble fiber forms a gel-like coating," she explains. Stirring again after five minutes prevents the seeds from clumping together or settling at the bottom of the jar. The mixture then goes into the refrigerator for at least one hour — though overnight yields the creamiest texture — until the chia seeds have fully hydrated and the pudding has thickened to a consistency resembling rice pudding.

The Indian Flavor Connection

What sets this apart from the generic chia puddings found at every wellness café is the spice profile. The combination of freshly ground green cardamom and saffron, two of the most prized aromatics in Indian cooking, connects it directly to desserts like mango kheer and aamrakhand (mango shrikhand). A garnish of crushed pistachios completes the reference.

Gupta recommends grinding cardamom at home rather than using store-bought powder, which can develop a musty taste over time. "Freshly ground green cardamom retains the bright, floral flavor that enhances the mango," she notes.

Nutrition and Versatility

At 272 calories per serving, the pudding delivers 10 grams of protein, 10 grams of fiber, and significant calcium (317 mg) and vitamin C (29 mg). The chia seeds contribute omega-3 fatty acids and help stabilize blood sugar, making it a more nutritionally complete option than many traditional mango desserts that rely on sugar and cream.

The recipe also adapts easily. A coconut variation uses light coconut milk and toasted coconut flakes. A mango lassi version substitutes part of the milk with Greek yogurt for extra protein. Plant-based milks work interchangeably with dairy, though Gupta suggests light coconut milk over full-fat to keep the pudding from becoming too heavy.

Practical Tips for Meal Prep

For families, the recipe scales linearly. The base keeps for up to four days refrigerated without toppings — the chopped mango and pistachios should be added just before serving to maintain freshness and crunch. Gupta advises against freezing, noting the texture becomes "gummy and stringy" after thawing.

Frozen mango works as a substitute when fresh is unavailable, and canned mango pulp can replace fresh fruit, though cooks should taste before adding sweetener since many brands are pre-sweetened. One small Ataulfo mango provides roughly half a cup of chopped fruit — enough for one serving with a little left over for garnish.

Whether served as a weekday grab-and-go breakfast or a light dessert after dinner, this mango chia pudding brings the familiar comfort of Indian mango desserts into a format that requires neither cooking skills nor time at the stove.
